breach.name: Nitro
breach.title: Nitro
breach.summary: In September 2020, the Nitro PDF service suffered a massive data breach which exposed over 70 million unique email addresses. The breach also exposed names, bcrypt password hashes and the titles of converted documents. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

background: In September 2020, the Nitro PDF service suffered a massive data breach which exposed over 70 million unique email addresses . The breach also exposed names, bcrypt password hashes and the titles of converted documents. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 77,159,696 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Names, Passwords.
editorial: The record mentions it almost in passing, and it is the most interesting thing in the entry: alongside the addresses and the bcrypt hashes, the breach exposed the titles of converted documents. Not the documents themselves. Their names. File names are content, written by people who assumed no one else would ever read them. "Offer letter final signed", "divorce petition draft 3", "Series A term sheet", "biopsy results", "redundancy list Q4".

Nobody names a private file euphemistically for their own benefit. A list of what seventy-seven million people were converting to PDF is therefore a map of what they were doing, legal trouble, job moves, medical news, deals in progress, indexed by email address and dated.

For companies that is targeting material of unusual quality: knowing an organisation converted a term sheet or a redundancy list in a particular week tells an attacker which pretext to use and exactly when to send it. For individuals it is an inference problem with no remedy. The password can be changed, and bcrypt probably held it anyway.
The title of a document you converted five years ago cannot be renamed after the fact.

fields.name: Passwords
fields.why: Anyone reusing this password elsewhere has those accounts exposed too, credential stuffing is automated and tries them all within days.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Change this password anywhere you reused it, starting with your email account, that is the one that can reset all the others.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is roughly everyone in the United Kingdom.
